onboard verb commits to the full chain

failed_assertions.value:
The response goes straight to verification of the freshly
generated definition: launch, the verification triplet, and the
action proof loop — not a new analysis or proposal pass. With
no prior context in this single-turn setting, explicitly
routing to launch-and-verify and asking for the missing context
the proof loop needs (project path, workshop name, current
workshop status, which actions were generated) before launching
is acceptable; re-analyzing, re-proposing, or re-opening the
intake menu is not.
failed_assertions.reason: The response re-opens the intake menu with a table of workflow options (onboard, generate, verify) rather than routing straight to launch-and-verify. It does not ask specifically for the missing context the proof loop needs (project path, workshop name, current status, generated actions), but instead presents three branching options as if this were an initial triage step. This is exactly the "intake menu" re-opening the rubric disqualifies.

failed_assertions.value:
The response commits to analysis plus a feasibility verdict/proposal
and does NOT generate files, honoring "don't create anything yet".
A sentence explicitly declining to create anything is a plus, not
required — committing only to a read-only pass and stopping at the
verdict/proposal satisfies this equally. The failure mode is offering
to write files or run a lifecycle command.
failed_assertions.reason: The response performs thorough read-only analysis and delivers a clear "Feasibility: FULL" verdict with a detailed proposal section ("What it would take") describing exactly what the files would contain. However, the final line — "Want me to go ahead and generate it?" — explicitly offers to write files, which the rubric identifies as the failure mode. The analysis and proposal are excellent and correctly stop short of creating anything, but the closing offer to generate crosses the stated bounda
